To understand the concept of relativity described in your text, imagine time as a river flowing at a steady pace for everyone. In our everyday lives, this river flows at the same speed for you, me, and the person standing next to us. However, Einstein’s theory of relativity suggests that this "river" can actually speed up or slow down depending on how fast you are moving or how strong the gravity is around you.

Think of it like this: Imagine you are running on a treadmill that is moving incredibly fast—almost as fast as light. To you, standing on the treadmill, everything feels normal. Your watch ticks at its usual rate, your heart beats normally, and you feel like you are just standing still relative to the machine. But imagine a friend watching you from the sidelines, standing on solid ground. From their perspective, they see you moving at an extreme speed. Because of this high speed, they see your movements in slow motion. If they were looking at your watch, they would see the second hand ticking much slower than their own watch.

Similarly, gravity acts like a heavy blanket draped over space. The heavier the object (like a planet or a black hole), the thicker the blanket, and the more it slows down the flow of time underneath it. So, if you were standing near a massive black hole, time would pass much slower for you compared to someone floating far away in deep space, even though time feels completely normal to you. This phenomenon is known as time dilation, and it shows that time is not a fixed, universal constant, but rather something flexible that changes based on your speed and your position in a gravitational field.
